desc:
Among all substrings of text (contiguous blocks, including the empty block), find the one that is closest to pattern in edit distance, and return that distance. The edit distance counts the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and replacements needed to turn one string into the other.

Equivalently: the fewest edits to pattern so that it occurs inside text.

text = "xxabcdxx", pattern = "abd"  ->  1   ("abc" or "abcd" is one edit away)
text = "aaaa",     pattern = "bbb"  ->  3
text = "",         pattern = "abc"  ->  3
text = "abc",      pattern = ""     ->  0   (the empty substring)
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Checking every substring with a full edit distance is far too slow: there are about n² substrings. Is there a way to share work between substrings that end at the same place?

In the ordinary table D[i][j] (first i pattern characters against some text prefix) the first row is D[0][j] = j because the whole text prefix has to be deleted. Which first row would let the match start anywhere for free?
Set D[0][j] = 0 for every j, keep the usual recurrence, and take the minimum of the last row D[m][j] over all j (the match may also end anywhere).
editorial: The standard recurrence aligns two whole strings. To allow the matched part of text to start at any position, make skipping a text prefix free by initialising the row for the empty pattern prefix to zeros: D[0][j] = 0. The column for an empty text prefix keeps its normal value D[i][0] = i, since the pattern characters still have to be produced. This idea is known as Sellers' algorithm.

Ending anywhere is handled at the end: the answer is the minimum over all columns of the last row, min_j D[m][j]. Skipping a text suffix is free in the same sense. The whole table has size m · n, and with a rolling array over the pattern index the memory is O(m). Trying all substrings separately would cost O(n² · m · n) or worse.
